title: 22. Interview: Sharding
summary: Interview Q&A for Sharding — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Sharding interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between sharding and partitioning?
**Answer:** Sharding and partitioning both split data into smaller pieces, but they differ in scope. Partitioning divides a table within a **single database** into smaller physical units (partitions) that share the same engine, memory, and disk — it is a storage optimization that stays invisible to the deployment topology. Sharding splits data across **multiple independent database servers**, each with its own CPU, memory, disk, and replication setup — it is a horizontal-scaling technique. A partitioned table can still fit on one machine; a sharded table cannot. Concretely: a PostgreSQL table partitioned by date into 12 monthly partitions lives on one server and queries transparently. The same table sharded by user_id across 16 servers requires a router that knows which server owns which user_id, and queries are 1-to-N network calls. Partitioning is the right answer when a single machine can hold the data but a single index becomes too large; sharding is the right answer when no single machine can hold the data or absorb the write rate. Many systems combine both — each shard is itself partitioned internally.
**Visual:**
```
PARTITIONING (1 machine):            SHARDING (N machines):
+--------------------------------+   +------+ +------+ +------+
| DB Server                      |   |Shard0| |Shard1| |Shard2|
|  table partitioned by date     |   | users| | users| | users|
|  p2023 p2024 p2025             |   | 0-1M | |1-2M  | |2-3M  |
+--------------------------------+   +------+ +------+ +------+
   (shared CPU/RAM/disk)             (independent servers)
```

### Q2. How do you choose a good shard key?
**Answer:** A good shard key has three properties. **High cardinality**: the key must have many distinct values so data spreads evenly. `user_id` (billions of values) is good; `country_code` (200 values, with skew toward the US and India) is bad — one shard will hold 80% of users. **Even write distribution**: avoid keys where writes concentrate on one value. An auto-incrementing `id` or `created_at` timestamp makes all new rows land on the highest range (range-based sharding) or hash bucket that happens to receive current writes — the "hot shard" problem. Use a hash of the key or a UUID to spread writes. **Query locality**: most application queries should filter by the shard key so they hit a single shard. Instagram shards by `user_id` because nearly every query ("show me user X's photos") filters by `user_id` — a single-shard O(1) lookup. If the most common query is "show me the latest photos globally," no shard key helps; you need a separate denormalized feed table. The fundamental tension: a single shard key cannot optimize every query pattern. Pick the one that fits the 99th-percentile hot query, and accept scatter-gather for the rest.
**Visual:**
```
GOOD shard key (user_id):           BAD shard key (country):
Shard0: users 0-1M   (even)         Shard0: US  (80% of traffic!)
Shard1: users 1-2M   (even)         Shard1: IN  (10%)
Shard2: users 2-3M   (even)         Shard2: others (10%)
-> all shards balanced              -> one shard overloaded
```

### Q3. What is consistent hashing and why is it used for sharding?
**Answer:** Consistent hashing places both nodes and keys on a circular hash ring (0 to 2^k). Each node owns the arc from its position clockwise to the next node. A key is placed on the node whose position is the first one clockwise from the key's hash. The crucial property: when a node is added or removed, only the keys in the affected arc move — typically 1/N of total data. With naive `hash(key) % N`, going from N to N+1 shards remaps roughly N/(N+1) of keys (almost everything). With consistent hashing, only ~1/(N+1) of keys move. This makes resharding a petabyte-scale cluster feasible: adding a 16th shard to a 15-shard cluster moves ~6% of data, not 94%. Consistent hashing also supports **virtual nodes** — each physical node appears at multiple positions on the ring (Cassandra uses 256 vnodes by default), smoothing the data distribution and ensuring that adding one node doesn't dump all its load on a single neighbor. Real-world users: Cassandra, DynamoDB, Redis Cluster, Akamai CDN, Discord (for routing voice channels). The trade-off is lookup complexity — O(log N) for a sorted ring vs O(1) for modulo — but this is negligible.
**Visual:**
```
Consistent hash ring (4 shards):
         shard-A
        /        \
   arc1            arc4
     /              \
shard-D            shard-B
     \              /
   arc3            arc2
        \        /
         shard-C
Add shard-E between A and B:
  only keys in arc4 (A->B clockwise) move to E
  ~1/5 of data moves, 4/5 stays put
```

### Q4. What is the hot shard problem and how do you mitigate it?
**Answer:** A hot shard emerges when the shard key has skew — a small number of key values receive disproportionate traffic. The classic example: a celebrity user (Justin Bieber on Instagram, Cristiano Ronaldo on Twitter) generates 1000× the read/write traffic of an average user. If their `user_id` hashes to shard 7, that shard is overloaded while 99% of the cluster is idle. Mitigations: (1) **Split the hot key across sub-shards** — instead of one row range for `user_id=42`, partition that user's data across multiple shards (e.g., `user_id=42, photos` on shard A, `user_id=42, comments` on shard B). The application routes based on (user_id, content_type). (2) **Directory override** — maintain a lookup table that explicitly maps known hot keys to dedicated "managed" shards with more capacity, bypassing the hash function. (3) **Replicate the hot shard** — add more read replicas for the hot shard so reads scale (writes still bottleneck on the primary). (4) **Application-level caching** — serve hot reads from Redis, reducing DB load. (5) **Salting the key** — append a random suffix (`user_id=42#0`, `user_id=42#1`, ...) so the key spreads across multiple hash buckets, at the cost of scatter-gather when reading. Uber uses key salting for hot city keys during peak hours.
**Visual:**
```
HOT SHARD:                       MITIGATION (salting):
shard7: user_42 (1000 QPS)       shard3: user_42#0 (250 QPS)
shard0-6,8-15: idle              shard7: user_42#1 (250 QPS)
                                 shard9: user_42#2 (250 QPS)
                                 shard2: user_42#3 (250 QPS)
                                 read user_42 -> scatter to 4 shards
```

### Q5. How do cross-shard transactions work and why are they hard?
**Answer:** A cross-shard transaction writes to multiple shards and needs atomicity — all commits or all roll back. The naive approach is **two-phase commit (2PC)**: a coordinator sends "prepare" to each shard, waits for all to ack, then sends "commit." If any shard fails to prepare, the coordinator aborts. 2PC is slow (multiple round trips), blocking (shards hold locks during prepare), and fragile (if the coordinator crashes, shards block indefinitely — the "blocking problem"). Most sharded systems forbid 2PC and instead use the **Saga pattern**: the transaction is broken into a sequence of single-shard sub-transactions, each with a compensating action. If sub-transaction 3 fails, the saga runs compensations for 1 and 2 to undo. This is eventually consistent — there's a window where the system is in an intermediate state — but it's resilient to failures and never blocks. Real-world: Amazon's order placement is a saga — reserve inventory, charge payment, create shipment, send confirmation — each step is a single-shard transaction, and a failure triggers compensations (release inventory, refund payment). The trade-off: 2PC gives you ACID across shards at the cost of latency and availability; Sagas give you availability at the cost of intermediate inconsistency. The right choice depends on whether you need cross-shard atomicity or can tolerate eventual consistency.
**Visual:**
```
2PC (slow, ACID):                SAGA (fast, eventual):
Coord --prepare--> S0,S1,S2      T1: write to S0 (commit)
S0,S1,S2 --ack--> Coord          T2: write to S1 (commit)
Coord --commit--> S0,S1,S2       T3: write to S2 (FAIL)
(blocking if coord crashes)      Compensate: undo T1, undo T2
                                 (no locks held, resilient)
```

### Q6. What is resharding and what are the strategies?
**Answer:** Resharding is the process of changing the number of shards — usually adding shards as data or traffic grows, occasionally removing them during a migration. The challenge is moving data without downtime. Strategies: (1) **Consistent hashing** — only ~1/N of keys move when adding one shard. The cluster routes reads to the old shard during migration, copies the affected keys to the new shard, then atomically switches the routing. (2) **Double the cluster** — going from N to 2N shards under `hash % N` only remaps 50% of keys, and each old shard splits in half. This is why many systems grow by powers of two (MongoDB chunks, Vitess shards). (3) **Vnodes** — each physical node hosts many virtual nodes on the ring; adding a physical node receives vnodes from multiple existing nodes, smoothing the load transfer. (4) **Online resharding** — run the old and new routing in parallel; writes go to both; reads prefer old until the new is fully populated; then cut over. Vitess and Citus support this. Real-world: Instagram has resharded its user data multiple times as it grew from millions to billions of users — each reshard took weeks of careful background data movement with dual-write consistency checks. The key principle: never do a "big bang" reshard; always migrate incrementally with a rollback path.
**Visual:**
```
Before: 4 shards                  After: 8 shards (double)
+------+ +------+ +------+ +------+   +--+ +--+ +--+ +--+ +--+ +--+ +--+ +--+
|Shard0| |Shard1| |Shard2| |Shard3|   |S0| |S0'| |S1| |S1'| |S2| |S2'| |S3| |S3'|
+------+ +------+ +------+ +------+   +--+ +--+ +--+ +--+ +--+ +--+ +--+ +--+
                                      each old shard splits in half
                                      only 50% of keys move (vs ~90% under +1)
```

### Q7. When should you NOT shard?
**Answer:** Sharding is expensive — operational complexity, code changes, query restrictions, and a permanent architectural commitment. Don't shard when alternatives work. (1) **Vertical scaling** still has headroom — a modern server with 64 cores, 2TB RAM, and 50TB NVMe can hold and serve a lot of data. PostgreSQL on such a box can handle terabytes and tens of thousands of QPS. (2) **Partitioning** (Topic 12) handles the case where a single table is too large but the data still fits on one machine — partition by date, get fast pruning, no app changes. (3) **Read replicas** (Topic 14) handle the case where reads are the bottleneck — add replicas, scale reads horizontally, keep one writer. (4) **Caching** (Redis) handles hot reads — 90% of reads to 1% of data can be served from cache. (5) **Archiving cold data** — move old rows to cheaper storage (S3, BigQuery) and keep the hot working set small. The rule of thumb: shard only when you have exhausted vertical scaling, partitioning, replicas, and caching — and you have a clear, measurable bottleneck that no other technique addresses. Premature sharding is a multi-year tax on developer productivity. Real-world: many startups shard early "for scale" and then spend years debugging cross-shard joins; better to defer until the data is genuinely too big for one machine.
**Visual:**
```
Try in order:
1. Bigger box (vertical scale)       -- cheap, simple
2. Partitioning (1 table -> N parts) -- no app change
3. Read replicas (scale reads)       -- 1 writer + N readers
4. Caching (hot reads in Redis)      -- 10-100x read speedup
5. Archive cold data (S3/warehouse)  -- shrink working set
6. SHARD (last resort)               -- expensive, permanent
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You're designing Instagram's photo storage. The user table is 1B rows and growing 100M/year. How would you shard it?
**Answer:** I'd shard by `user_id` using consistent hashing across, say, 64 shards to start, with each shard being a PostgreSQL primary + 2 read replicas. The shard key is `user_id` because virtually every query is scoped to a user — "show me user X's photos," "show me user X's followers" — and a single-shard lookup is O(1). I'd use a directory-based router (a Vitess-style proxy or an in-app client with a cached routing table) that maps `user_id → shard` via consistent hashing. Each shard holds ~15M users and ~150M photos. I'd pre-provision 2x headroom so the cluster can grow to 128 shards via doubling when any shard hits 70% capacity. For the celebrity hot-shard problem (Justin Bieber), I'd maintain a directory override list of "managed users" who get dedicated shards or sub-sharded across multiple shards via key salting. For global feed queries ("latest photos from people I follow"), I'd maintain a separate denormalized `feed` table (per-user timeline, precomputed by a fanout worker) — the sharded `photos` table is the source of truth, but the feed reads from a per-user precomputed list. For media files, I'd use S3 with the photo ID as the key — S3 handles its own sharding internally. Resharding would happen via online dual-write with background data copy, taking weeks per reshard event.
**Visual:**
```
+-------+    +-------------------+
|  App  |--->| Shard Router      |
+-------+    | hash(user_id) %64 |
             +---+--+--+--+------+
                 |  |  |  |
              64 shards (PostgreSQL primary + 2 replicas each)
              each shard: ~15M users, ~150M photos

Celebrity: directory override -> dedicated "managed" shard
Global feed: separate denormalized feed table (fanout-on-write)
```

### Q2. Uber needs to store trip data — billions of trips, immutable once completed, but heavy real-time reads for in-progress trips. How do you shard?
**Answer:** I'd shard by `trip_id` (a UUID) using consistent hashing across a Cassandra cluster — Cassandra is a natural fit because trips are time-series-ish, immutable after completion, and writes are append-only. The shard key is `trip_id` rather than `driver_id` or `rider_id` because: (1) `trip_id` has perfect cardinality (every trip is unique) and even distribution; (2) the hottest query — "show me the current state of trip X" — is `WHERE trip_id=?`, a single-shard lookup; (3) historical queries ("show me all trips for driver Y") can scatter-gather across all shards and are not latency-sensitive. For in-progress trips, I'd use a separate hot store (Redis) keyed by `trip_id` with a TTL of 24 hours — every update (location ping, status change) writes to both Redis (fast read for live trip view) and Cassandra (durable). When the trip completes, the Cassandra row is finalized and the Redis entry expires. The Cassandra cluster would have 256 vnodes per node for even distribution and RF=3 (three replicas) for durability. Resharding happens automatically as vnodes rebalance — Cassandra handles this natively. For analytics ("how many trips in SF last hour"), I'd maintain a separate precomputed aggregate in Kafka Streams or a real-time OLAP store (Druid, ClickHouse) fed by CDC — never run analytics on the operational Cassandra cluster.
**Visual:**
```
Trip event (location ping):
  -> Redis (hot, sub-ms, TTL 24h)    [for live trip view]
  -> Cassandra (durable, RF=3)        [for history]
  -> Kafka -> Druid                   [for analytics]

Cassandra: consistent hashing, 256 vnodes/node
  trip_id (UUID) -> ring lookup -> shard
  in-progress reads: O(1) shard lookup
  analytics: separate Druid cluster (never scatter on Cassandra)
```

### Q3. Netflix's viewing history is 250M users × 50 videos = 12.5B rows. Reads dominate 100:1 over writes. Do you shard or use another approach?
**Answer:** Given the 100:1 read-to-write ratio, sharding alone is the wrong first move — caching and denormalization deliver more value per dollar. My approach: (1) Keep a normalized `viewing_history` table in PostgreSQL, partitioned by `user_id` hash into 32 partitions (single-machine, no app changes — Topic 12). This is the system of record. (2) Maintain a denormalized "continue watching" read model in Cassandra, keyed by `user_id` and sorted by `last_watched_at DESC` — each row contains video metadata (title, thumbnail, position) so reads are a single partition scan, sub-10ms. (3) Put a Redis cache in front of Cassandra for the top 10% of active users — sub-millisecond reads, hit rate ~95%. (4) Replicate PostgreSQL to read replicas for ad-hoc queries and analytics. This handles 100k reads/sec on the "continue watching" path with no joins. If the PostgreSQL write rate becomes a bottleneck later (unlikely at 100:1), I'd revisit sharding — but at 250M users and modest writes per user, a single PostgreSQL primary with partitioning handles it. The Cassandra layer scales horizontally (already sharded by `user_id`), and Redis adds another horizontal layer. Real-world: Netflix actually uses this pattern — Cassandra for viewing history, EVCache (their Redis fork) for hot reads, PostgreSQL for billing/identity.
**Visual:**
```
App --read--> Redis (cache, 95% hit) --miss--> Cassandra (denormalized)
                                                  ^
                                                  | CDC
App --write--> PostgreSQL (normalized, partitioned)
                |
                +--> read replicas (analytics)

Why no sharding of PostgreSQL? 100:1 read:write -> cache/replica solve it
Cassandra is already sharded internally (by user_id)
```

### Q4. WhatsApp handles 100B messages/day with 2B users. How would you shard the messages table?
**Answer:** I'd shard by `conversation_id` (a hash of sorted participant IDs), not by `user_id` or `message_id`. Rationale: virtually every WhatsApp query is "show me the messages in conversation X" — a single conversation's messages must be on the same shard to avoid scatter-gather. If I sharded by `user_id`, a conversation between Alice and Bob would have Alice's messages on her shard and Bob's messages on his shard — fetching the conversation would require merging two shards and sorting by timestamp. Sharding by `conversation_id` puts all messages for a conversation on one shard, and the query becomes `WHERE conversation_id=? ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 50` — a single-shard lookup. I'd use consistent hashing across, say, 1024 shards (WhatsApp's scale demands thousands), with each shard being a MySQL primary + replicas (WhatsApp famously runs MySQL at scale). Each conversation averages ~1000 messages, so a shard with 1M conversations holds ~1B messages — large but manageable with proper indexing. For media (photos, videos), I'd use S3 with a content-addressed key (hash of content) for dedup. For delivery status (sent/delivered/read), I'd maintain a separate per-recipient status table, also sharded by `conversation_id`. The hot-shard risk: a group chat with 256 members generates 256 status updates per message — mitigate by batching status updates and writing them asynchronously via Kafka. WhatsApp actually does this — Erlang-based message brokers, MySQL shards, and ~50 engineers supporting 2B users.
**Visual:**
```
conversation_id = hash(sorted([alice_id, bob_id]))
  -> all msgs for this conversation on ONE shard

Shard X: conversation_42 msgs
  msg_id | conv_id | sender | text | ts
  1      | 42      | alice  | hi   | 10:00
  2      | 42      | bob    | hey  | 10:01

Read conversation: SELECT * FROM msgs WHERE conv_id=42 ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 50
  -> 1 shard lookup, no scatter-gather
```

### Q5. YouTube receives 500 hours of video uploaded per minute. How would you shard the video metadata table (not the video bytes)?
**Answer:** I'd separate video bytes (in a CDN/object store like S3, which handles its own sharding) from video metadata (title, uploader, duration, views, likes) in a sharded database. Shard key: `video_id` (a YouTube-style 11-char base64 ID like `dQw4w9WgXcQ`). Rationale: `video_id` has perfect cardinality (every video is unique), even distribution (random IDs), and the hottest query — "show me video X's metadata" — is `WHERE video_id=?`, a single-shard lookup. I'd use consistent hashing across ~256 shards (Cassandra or Vitess-sharded MySQL). For the upload path, the metadata write and the video-byte upload are separate: the upload service reserves a `video_id` first (single-shard write to the metadata DB), then uploads bytes to S3, then updates the metadata row with the S3 URL and processing status. For the watch path, the metadata DB serves the video info card, and the CDN serves the bytes. For "trending" or "recommendations," I'd maintain separate denormalized read models — a Redis sorted set of trending video IDs per region, refreshed every minute by a stream processor; the metadata lookup happens after the recommendation (fetch 20 video_ids → 20 single-shard lookups in parallel). For "show me all videos by channel X," I'd maintain a secondary index: `channel_id → [video_id, video_id, ...]` in a separate keyspace, sharded by `channel_id`. The key principle: `video_id` is the primary shard key for the metadata table; secondary access patterns use denormalized indexes, not scatter-gather.
**Visual:**
```
Upload:
  1. reserve video_id -> shard(video_id) write (status=uploading)
  2. upload bytes to S3
  3. update metadata row (status=ready, s3_url=...)

Watch:
  App -> CDN (video bytes, 99% cache hit)
  App -> metadata DB -> shard(video_id) -> 1 lookup (info card)

Trending:
  Stream processor -> Redis sorted set (per region, refreshed/min)
  App -> Redis (top 20 video_ids) -> metadata DB (20 parallel lookups)
```

### Q6. Amazon's product catalog has 350M products. Searches are full-text and faceted (by category, brand, price). How do you shard?
**Answer:** I'd separate the catalog storage from the search index — they have different access patterns and different optimal data structures. For storage: a sharded PostgreSQL or DynamoDB keyed by `product_id`, with ~64 shards via consistent hashing. This is the system of record — writes go here (price updates, inventory changes, new products). For search: an Elasticsearch cluster with the product data denormalized into documents (`{product_id, title, description, category, brand, price, attributes, ...}`), sharded by `product_id` hash across, say, 100 ES shards. Search queries (`title:iphone AND category:electronics AND price:<1000`) run via Elasticsearch's distributed query — ES internally scatter-gathers across its shards and merges, returning ranked results in tens of milliseconds. Updates flow from PostgreSQL to Elasticsearch via CDC (Debezium → Kafka → ES indexer), with eventual consistency of a few seconds — acceptable for search (a price update taking 5 seconds to appear in search results is fine; a price appearing wrong at checkout is not, so checkout reads from PostgreSQL directly). For the "product detail page" — the most-read path — I'd cache the rendered page in Redis with a 5-minute TTL, hitting PostgreSQL only on cache miss. The shard key choice (`product_id`) is universal across the three stores (PostgreSQL, ES, Redis), making correlation easy. The trade-off: 3x storage (PostgreSQL + ES + Redis cache), but each store is optimized for its access pattern — and Amazon's catalog at this scale demands it.
**Visual:**
```
Write (price update):
  App -> PostgreSQL (shard by product_id) [system of record]
          |
          v  CDC (Debezium -> Kafka)
  Elasticsearch (denormalized docs, shard by product_id hash)
          |
          v  invalidate
  Redis cache (rendered product page, TTL 5min)

Search: App -> ES (scatter-gather, ranked results)
PDP:    App -> Redis (cache) -> PG on miss
Checkout: App -> PostgreSQL directly (strong read)
```

### Q7. You're migrating a 10TB single-PostgreSQL database to a sharded cluster with no downtime. Walk me through the plan.
**Answer:** Zero-downtime migration requires dual-write + online data copy + cutover. **Phase 1: Set up the new cluster** — provision N shards (e.g., 16) with consistent hashing, empty schemas, replicas, monitoring. **Phase 2: Schema and routing** — deploy a shard router that can route by `shard_key` to the new cluster; it returns "not found" for now. **Phase 3: Dual-write** — modify the application to write to both the old single DB and the new sharded cluster, with the new write in a fire-and-forget async path (don't block on it). Reads still go to the old DB. **Phase 4: Backfill** — run a background job that copies existing rows from the old DB to the new shards in chunks (e.g., 1000 rows at a time, ordered by `shard_key`), with rate limiting to avoid overloading the old DB. Use the dual-write log to handle concurrent updates — if a row was already written by dual-write, skip it. **Phase 5: Verification** — run a continuous reconciliation job that compares row counts and checksums between old and new; fix discrepancies. **Phase 6: Shadow reads** — route 1% of reads to the new cluster and compare results with the old; if they match, ramp to 10%, 50%, 100%. **Phase 7: Cutover** — switch all reads to the new cluster; keep dual-write on for 24 hours as a safety net. **Phase 8: Decommission** — stop dual-write, drop the old DB. Each phase takes days to weeks; the whole migration is typically 1-3 months. Vitess and Citus have tooling for this; if rolling your own, the verification step is the most important — never cut over without it.
**Visual:**
```
Phase 3:              Phase 4:             Phase 6:
App --write--> Old     App --write--> Old    App --read--> Old (99%)
      \\--> New              \\--> New            \\--> New (1% shadow)
                       Backfill job:
                       Old -> chunked -> New
                       (rate-limited, idempotent)

Phase 7: cutover      Phase 8: decommission
App --write--> New     App --write--> New  (Old dropped)
      \\--> Old (safety)  
App --read--> New
```

quiz.explanation: two-phase commit (2PC): a coordinator sends "prepare" to each shard, waits for all to ack, then sends "commit." If any shard fails to prepare, the coordinator aborts. 2PC is slow (multiple round trips), blocking (shards hold locks during prepare), and fragile (if the coordinator crashes, shards block indefinitely — the "blocking problem").
